processing: Mainly steamed as sencha; small producers have also made hand-processed black tea from it.
harvest_season: Extremely early spring: up to two days before Kuritawase and roughly two weeks ahead of Yabukita.
appearance_dry: Dark green rolled needles, as is typical of sencha.
appearance_liquor: Clear yellow-green, as is typical of sencha.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf, as is typical of steamed sencha.
taste_profile: Sweet and fresh, with some astringency attributed to the Assam blood in its ancestry.

brewing.notes: Keep the water moderate; the astringency shows quickly in a hot or long steep.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, and because it comes in so early it suits the first shincha of the year from southern Japan. Drink it within about a year; rare single-cultivar black tea versions are also small seasonal lots.
description:
Shuntarou is about timing. It is one of Japan's earliest cultivars, ready even a little before Kuritawase and well ahead of Yabukita, which is valuable to growers in the far south who aim to bring the first new tea to market.

It dislikes cold and belongs in southern Japan. Most of it goes into sencha, though a producer on Tanegashima also sells it as a hand-made black tea, a reminder that it carries Assam-type genes.

As sencha it tastes sweet and fresh with a little grip. Watch the temperature and the clock, since that astringency arrives quickly.

Yields beat Kuritawase but remain low compared with other cultivars, so it is not a common name on a pack. Look for it from Kagoshima and Tanegashima sellers, and compare a sencha with the black tea version if you find both.
history:
Shuntarou comes from NARO's Makurazaki branch in Kagoshima. One account traces it to a 1990 cross between Saitama 9 and Makura F1-33422, itself a hybrid of Kuritawase and Benitachiwase; the application for registration was published in June 2009.

Breeders report very strong resistance to gray blight, fair resistance to anthracnose and slight weakness against white peach scale.
